newsitem.title: UK: One quarter of UK windfall cash to be spent-survey.
newsitem.headline: One quarter of UK windfall cash to be spent-survey.

text.p: Just under a quarter of the windfall cash paid out this year by British building societies to households will be spent, boosting economic growth by 0.5 percent, a survey said on Monday.
The survey, conducted by consumer analysis group Mintel by Robert Fleming Securities, questioned 3,000 recipients of windfall cash from the first four big flotations.

It found around 23 percent, or 8.2 billion pounds, of the 30 billion pounds of free shares issued so far has already or will be spent, with 2.1 billion going on home improvements and furnishings, 2.1 billion on holidays and travel and 700 million on electrical items for the home.

"Taking into account the other windfalls, the overall impact of higher consumer spending is likely to boost the value of GDP by about 0.5 percent this year and 0.1 percent next year," said Peter Warburton, economic adviser at Robert Fleming Securities.
The impact would have been greater but for the high content of spending on import goods associated with the windfalls, he added.
He said the survey also found that only 13 percent of respondents indicated their new-found spending confidence would continue at the exponse of saving.

"The surge in consumer confidence, which has occured during the last six months as these windfall payments have been eagerly awaited, is therefore likely to be reversed quite rapidly this autumn," Warburton said.
If this happens, it will be welcome news for the Bank of England which increased the cost of borrowing to 7.0 percnet last week to try and dampen demand among consumers.
Extra spending on home improvements will boost turnover in that sector by 8.0 percent over last year, by 9.0 percent on holidays and travel and by 6.0 percent on consumer durables.
The remaining 77 percent will be saved or used to repay existing debt, the survey said.

Of those who intend to save all or some of their windfalls, 60 percent will hold their shares in their own name, 16 percent in a personal equity plan (PEP) or invest the sale proceeds on a PEP, unit trust or other stock market vehicle.
A further 17 percent will sell their shares and hold the proceeds on deposit with a bank or building society.
This translates into 4.0 billion pounds of new business for the PEP and unit trust business and a further four billion pounds of new deposits for banks and building societies.
